idiom_name: in-class one-line member (implicitly inline); using-declaration to re-expose inherited names
implementation_notes: A member function defined inside the class body is implicitly inline, so the one-line forwarder is the language's ordinary shape and the compiler can see through it at -O2: explicit inline or [[gnu::always_inline]] only add a hint that may be ignored, and neither can force a virtual call to be inlined. When the goal is only to un-hide a base-class member rather than to rename or narrow it, a using-declaration (using Base::f;) re-exposes every base overload with no body at all - that declaration is the closest thing C++ has to a replacement for the classic structure, but it cannot forward to a composed field and it keeps the original name, so the pattern's naming half is always hand-written.
pitfalls: using Base::f; only re-exposes inherited members: it silently reopens the whole overload set and keeps the base name, so callers gain no intention-revealing vocabulary.
A one-line forwarder that returns by value copies unless the delegate returns a reference; use decltype(auto) or a forwarding reference when the wrapper must be distribution-transparent.
Inlining hints cannot be enforced and are ignored across virtual dispatch boundaries; keep the wrapper non-virtual where possible so the compiler can see the delegated call.
